newsitem.title: RUSSIA: FOCUS - Russian central bank sees fall in yields.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Russian central bank sees fall in yields.

text.p: A senior Russian central banker said on Wednesday that financial markets were under control and forecast a sharp fall in yields on government securities.
Russian markets have been unnerved recently by an increase in rouble liquidity due to foreign buying of Treasury bills and the sale of Russia's first Eurobond last November.
As a result the central bank was forced to mop up roubles by selling dollars, running down its reserves.
"The Central Bank is in full control of the financial markets," First Deputy Chairman Sergei Aleksashenko told Reuters Financial Television.

"We control the reserves and have the ability to bring about a long-term decrease in yields on Russian paper, and we predict that yields on T-bills will soon become closer to that of the dollar-denominated Eurobond."

The 9.25 percent 2001 Eurobond currently yields about 9.55 percent, while T-bills maturing in June-August this year are yielding 27-28 percent. Russian inflation is forecast to slow to 12 percent this year from 21.8 percent in 1996.
The central bank sold $1.5 billion of currency reserves in January after buying several hundred million dollars in December, Aleksashenko said.
But the situation had changed in the first days of February and the Central Bank was now only buying hard currency, he said. Its reserves are now over $10 billion, he said.
Under Russia's crawling peg policy the rouble, trading on Wednesday at about 5,650 per dollar, should be in a 5,750-6,350 per dollar range on December 31, 1997.

The authorities have been holding the rouble in a corridor since the middle of 1995. The rouble has never strayed from inside the corridor or the bid/offer rates set within the corridor by the central bank since summer last year.
But a faster than usual depreciation in the rouble last summer worried investors and pushed up T-bill yields.
Non-resident demand for Russian government paper has risen significantly in recent weeks.
Yields have fallen from about 200 percent annual in early 1996, but are still much higher than returns in other markets.
Aleksashenko said non-residents were investing about $1 billion monthly in January and February into GKO discount Treasury bills.
Aleksashenko said most foreigners would not be affected by a new 15 percent tax on government securities, as their profits on the income are covered by double taxation treaties.
